record.text:
The ratio loss is introduced to prevent the model from collapsing to trivial solutions that either keep almost all vectors (eliminating any computational gain) or over‑compress them and lose essential information, a problem analogous to expert‑utilization imbalance in Mixture‑of‑Experts models【S2】.  
It formalizes a target compression ratio by penalising the mismatch between the actual fraction of selected vectors ( F ) and the average boundary probability ( G ), using the hyper‑parameter N that encodes the desired compression level【S2】.  
F is defined as the average over a sequence of the binary selection indicators bₜ, i.e., the proportion of vectors that are actually retained after the routing decision【S2】.  
G is the mean of the boundary probabilities pₜ produced by the routing module, providing a continuous signal that can be back‑propagated to steer the model toward the target ratio【S2】.  
N controls the target compression ratio: when F = G = 1⁄N, the ratio loss reaches its minimum value of 1, encouraging the model to achieve the intended compression factor【S2】.  
Thus, by jointly optimizing the autoregressive prediction loss and the ratio loss (scaled by α), the network learns content‑adaptive compression while adhering to a prescribed compression budget【S2】.

Inner Monologue is a method that generates text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens within Moshi’s hierarchical multi‑stream language model, while remaining compatible with streaming inference【S2】.  
By inserting a configurable delay between the text sequence and the audio token sequence, the model can be made to let either the audio dictate the text (for ASR) or the text dictate the audio (for TTS) without changing the loss, architecture, or training data【S3】.  
For streaming ASR, the text tokens are delayed (e.g., by 2 s) so that the model listens to audio before emitting text, and during inference the audio tokens are teacher‑forced while the model predicts the delayed text tokens, yielding word‑level alignments【S1】【S3】.  
For streaming TTS, the audio tokens are delayed (e.g., by 2 s) so that the model receives text ahead of the audio and predicts the delayed audio tokens, while the ground‑truth text tokens are teacher‑forced at inference, enabling low‑latency speech synthesis【S1】【S3】.  
Both configurations use the same underlying model and only differ by the chosen delay hyper‑parameter, allowing a single system to switch between streaming ASR and streaming TTS【S1】【S3】.

record.text: Scaled dot‑product attention takes each query vector, computes its dot product with every key vector to measure similarity, and then uses those scores to weight a sum of the corresponding value vectors [S1][S2]. The raw dot products can become large when the key dimension \(d_k\) is high, because the variance of a sum of \(d_k\) independent components grows proportionally to \(d_k\) [S1]. To keep the softmax from falling into regions with extremely small gradients, the dot products are divided by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) before the softmax is applied [S1]. This scaling normalizes the magnitude of the scores, yielding more stable gradients and better training dynamics [S1].

Scaled dot‑product attention first takes each query vector and computes its dot product with every key vector, forming a matrix of similarity scores; these scores are divided by √d_k, passed through a softmax to obtain attention weights, and then used to take a weighted sum of the corresponding value vectors [S1][S2].

H‑Net determines chunk boundaries with a learned routing module that outputs a binary indicator bₜ for each byte, where bₜ = 1 marks a cut point; this module is trained end‑to‑end together with the backbone so that the positions of bₜ reflect the data’s semantic structure rather than fixed heuristics [S1].  
In practice the model learns to place most cuts at whitespace characters in a single‑stage setting, because word boundaries naturally correspond to meaningful units [S2].  
When a second hierarchical stage is added, the first stage still focuses on spacelike bytes but also tends to cut after the initial characters of each word, allowing the remaining characters to be predicted more easily [S2].  
Beyond simple whitespace, H‑Net’s boundaries are content‑aware: it frequently merges adjacent words or punctuation into a single chunk when the surrounding context makes them semantically cohesive [S2].  
Perturbation experiments show that even when spaces are removed, the routing module continues to insert cuts between semantic words, confirming that boundary decisions depend on contextual meaning rather than static byte patterns [S2].

record.text: Inner Monologue is a new method introduced in Moshi that generates text tokens as a prefix to the audio tokens while remaining compatible with streaming inference [S2]. By inserting a controllable delay between the generated text sequence (Wₜ) and the corresponding audio tokens (Aₜ, q), the language model can be made to decide the content of one modality based on the other [S3]. If the audio tokens are generated ahead of the text, sampling only the text tokens while feeding ground‑truth audio tokens yields a streaming automatic‑speech‑recognition system with precise word‑level alignment [S3]. Conversely, by delaying the text tokens so that they lead the audio tokens, the model’s audio output is driven by the text, producing a streaming text‑to‑speech system [S3]. This single delay hyper‑parameter therefore lets the same model switch between streaming ASR and streaming TTS without any changes to its loss, architecture, or training data [S2][S3].

Inner Monologue is a method introduced in Moshi that generates text tokens as a prefix to audio tokens, allowing the same language‑model architecture to be used for both speech‑to‑text and text‑to‑speech tasks while remaining compatible with streaming inference【S2】.  
By inserting a controllable delay between the text sequence (Wₜ) and the audio tokens (Aₜ,q), the model can be made to decide the content of one modality based on the other【S3】.  
If the audio tokens are delayed (e.g., by 2 seconds) and the model is forced to use ground‑truth audio tokens while predicting only text tokens, it functions as a streaming ASR system that also yields precise word‑level alignments【S1】【S3】.  
Conversely, when the text tokens are delayed and the model is forced to use ground‑truth text tokens while predicting audio tokens, it becomes a streaming TTS system that can synthesize speech with only a short look‑ahead (2 seconds)【S1】【S3】.  
Both configurations use the same loss, architecture, and training data; the only change is the delay hyper‑parameter that switches the model between ASR and TTS modes【S1】【S3】.  
Experiments show that with a 2‑second look‑ahead the streaming TTS achieves 4.7 % WER on LibriSpeech test‑clean and the streaming ASR achieves 5.7 % WER, illustrating the flexibility of Inner Monologue for real‑time speech applications【S1】.

record.text: H‑Net learns to place chunk boundaries by a routing module that predicts a binary boundary indicator \(b_t\in\{0,1\}\) for each input byte, conditioned on the full contextual embedding of that position [S1]. The routing module is jointly trained with the rest of the network so that the chosen boundaries minimise the downstream loss, making the segmentation data‑dependent and context‑aware [S1]. In practice, a single‑stage H‑Net tends to place boundaries at whitespace characters, effectively learning that word boundaries are natural semantic units, while a two‑stage H‑Net first marks spacelike bytes and the initial characters of words before the second stage merges these into larger semantic chunks such as whole words or phrases [S3]. The model therefore does not rely on fixed delimiters or external heuristics; instead it adapts its cut points to the content and context of the sequence during end‑to‑end training [S3]. This dynamic chunking is achieved without any explicit supervision on boundary labels, relying instead on the differentiable routing and downsampling operations within the network [S1].

H-Net decides where to cut the byte stream by using a routing module that dynamically draws chunk boundaries based on contextual information [S1]. This routing module generates binary boundary indicators, allowing the system to compress input vectors into meaningful chunks without external supervision [S1]. In hierarchical two-stage designs, the first stage combines these spacelike boundaries with the initial characters of each word to aid prediction [S3]. The chunking process is content-aware, meaning it can merge multiple words into a single chunk if they form a coherent semantic group, regardless of static rules [S3]. These boundaries are determined by the specific content and context of the input, rather than relying on fixed heuristics or delimiters [S3].

The ratio loss is a regularizer that encourages H‑Net to achieve a specified compression ratio by penalising the discrepancy between the actual fraction of retained vectors \(F\) and the average boundary probability \(G\), scaled by a target ratio parameter \(N\)【S1】.  
\(F\) is defined as the mean selection rate over a sequence, i.e. the fraction of vectors that are actually kept by the routing module【S1】.  
\(G\) is the mean boundary probability across the sequence, reflecting how often the model predicts a boundary (i.e. discards a vector)【S1】.  
\(N\) controls the desired compression ratio; when \(F=G=\frac{1}{N}\) the ratio loss is minimized, driving the model toward the target ratio【S1】.
